compression.title: IPTC Metawatch
compression.lede: is the IPTC's free, open monthly monitor of whether news publishers keep the photo metadata embedded in their images: 508 publishers in 122 countries, the lead photograph of up to 20 recent articles each, scored on creator, caption, copyright and credit line.

sentences.text: IPTC Metawatch is the International Press Telecommunications Council's free, open monitor of whether news publishers keep the credits, captions and rights information embedded in their photographs, checked every month across more than 500 publishers in 122 countries (IPTC announcement, 5 October 2026); the provenance census record types it as a monitor of the media lineage whose capability is to test, its provenance object 'the lead photograph of a news article, as served to the reader', its operator the IPTC at metawatch.iptc.org (provenance census record).

Its own overview states the object from the side of the carrier: Metawatch 'tracks how often major news publishers preserve embedded photo metadata' — Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata in its IIM and XMP forms, and C2PA — and scores the photographs a curated list of publishers serves (Metawatch overview), the carrier the census record names as 'embedded metadata (Exif, IPTC IIM and XMP) and C2PA manifests' (provenance census record).

Content Credentials stand in the first of the dimensions of provenance the archive's provenance packet distinguishes: frameworks for the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and for the corpus 'are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis', artifact provenance verifying that 'this file' was created by 'this source' at 'this time', at the moment of creation (#725); the same packet places IPTC AI metadata at 'Layer 1 metadata', 'Disclosure, not lineage' (#725).

On the first of each month its crawler visits 508 news publishers in 122 countries, takes up to 20 recent articles from each and reads the lead photograph of every article, checking Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata and C2PA Content Credentials and scoring creator, caption, copyright and credit line, 'the “4 Cs”' (IPTC announcement); the census record's unit is 'a news publisher, sampled each month through up to 20 recent articles', its count 508 publishers in 122 countries as of October 2026, monthly on the first, its relation types creator, credit, copyright, caption, the PLUS data-mining preference and Content Credentials (provenance census record); the per-field page calls the four scored fields 'the "Four Cs" of news photo provenance', the others tracked for context (Metawatch per-field breakdown).

The crawler is 'deliberately light', about 40 to 60 requests per publisher a month, honouring robots.txt and keeping no article text or image files, and every run is published as open data under CC BY 4.0, new results appearing on the first of every month (IPTC announcement); the overview names it 'A project of the International Press Telecommunications Council', its data CC BY 4.0, with an opt-out for publishers by email (Metawatch overview), and the census record carries 'every run published as open data' under 'CC BY 4.0 (each run's data)' (provenance census record).

What it tests is a transformation: credits 'are lost between camera and reader' as content management systems re-encode images, delivery networks resize them and optimisation tools discard what looks like unnecessary bytes, and once an image is copied or collected by an AI crawler its embedded metadata 'is often the only record of where it came from and on what terms it may be used' (IPTC announcement); the census record names the transformation tested 'publication through a news site's pipeline (CMS, CDN, image optimisation)' (provenance census record).

The archive's packet states the loss one layer on: 'A C2PA-signed image whose caption is rewritten by a model that strips the photographer's name has lost semantic provenance even though artifact provenance is preserved', the dimensions being independent, so that 'Solving any one dimension does not solve the others' (#725).

Metawatch builds on IMATAG's 2018 State of Image Metadata study and the IPTC's own prototype crawler of 2019, and differs in measuring every month (IPTC announcement; the census record quotes the sentence as its lineage evidence, provenance census record), and the census record relates it as part of the IPTC's photo-metadata tests, beside the census's C2PA conformance entry, while keeping it apart from the earlier test: 'NOT the 2019 IPTC social-media test: it measures news publishers monthly' (provenance census record).

Its overview dates five runs, the first on 2026-06-03 and then monthly to 2026-10-01 (Metawatch overview), and the announcement counts 294 publishers 'measured every month since June' (IPTC announcement).

The IPTC's post of 8 September 2026 reports that at the 2026 Photo Metadata Conference, held 'Last Thursday', Brendan Quinn 'appeared again to introduce Metawatch', 'IPTC’s new public service that monitors real-world usage of metadata in images across the global news industry, tracking IPTC/XMP, C2PA, AI opt-outs and more' (IPTC, 8 September 2026); Paul Melcher's LinkedIn post of 14 September 2026, read by its card alone, says the IPTC 'now publishes Metawatch' (LinkedIn card); the conference took as its focus AI transparency and content provenance, 'tracking real-world adoption of content transparency technologies by AI engines, news sites, software and services' (IPTC, 8 September 2026).

The announcement is dated 5 October 2026 and is the newest post under the IPTC's Photo Metadata tag (IPTC announcement; Photo Metadata archive); the census record's lifecycle is active, 'announced 5 October 2026', its founding given the same way, the run reported for October 2026 and the record read on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record).

The Capture Registry records the difference: the record 'dates the monitor by its announcement, 5 October 2026', two cards date it earlier, the IPTC post of 8 September and Melcher's post of 14 September, and the September showing is carried at the capture 'unchecked against the posts themselves' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

In the October run 7.2% of editorial images carried a credit or copyright notice, against IMATAG's 8% in 2018, so that keeping the photographer's credit attached 'has not improved'; 321 of the 425 publishers it could crawl kept none of the scored IPTC fields; 11% of 6,580 images carried any IPTC metadata, the photographer's name on 7.9%, the credit line on 5.7%, copyright on 5.6% (IPTC announcement); the census record's retention results carry the 7.2% and the 321 of 425 with the 27 of 6,580 images bearing a C2PA manifest (provenance census record), and the announcement reads its first results as showing 'how little has changed since 2018' and why metadata 'matters more than ever now that AI companies are crawling the web' (IPTC announcement).

The overview gives the latest run as 2026-10-01, 425 sites, 122 countries and 6,580 images, a mean IPTC score of 5.96, 11% with any IPTC and 0.5% with C2PA, and says that 'Any average describes almost nobody here' (Metawatch overview); the per-field page counts over 6,514 images, Creator at 7.9%, CreditLine 5.7%, Copyright 5.3%, CaptionDescription 5%, the licensing fields below 3% (Metawatch per-field breakdown), so that copyright stands at 5.6% in the announcement and at 5.3% on the per-field page.

On where the loss happens the operator's pages differ in emphasis: the announcement finds 'It isn’t the CDN’s fault', images through Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront and Fastly losing their metadata 87% to 95% of the time and images with no CDN 87%, so that 'Stripping appears to happen in the publishing pipeline', the fix 'usually a setting, not a project' (IPTC announcement; the census record quotes the pipeline sentence as its evidence, provenance census record), while the per-field page reads its dataset as 'publishers and CDNs are discarding metadata that the photographers and agencies almost certainly embedded upstream' (Metawatch per-field breakdown).

The archive's specification for machine-eligible handwritten artifacts embeds IPTC Creator (the author or heteronym), Credit, CopyrightNotice, Headline, Description and DateCreated in every published derivative, with an XMP mirror and C2PA manifests wrapping the IPTC/EXIF assertions (#1409); it records embedded IPTC photo metadata as extracted by Google and travelling with the image, its composition role unknown, 'scaffold the pipeline provably reads' (#1409); and it carries the same fields in a visible membrane because 'physically embodied metadata survives screenshot, rehosting, filename change, metadata stripping, PDF embedding, and sidecar loss', under a triple redundancy of pixels, embedded IPTC/XMP/C2PA and external records (#1409).

The archive's identifier stamp for a lossless image sits in its EXIF ImageDescription or UserComment (#1432), and its self-audit protocol plans a 'Hash/signature manifest (C2PA-compatible) binding provenance claims to deposited objects' (#204).

Some publishers moved: USA Today from no credit metadata in 2019 to 95% of its lead photographs carrying credit, creator and copyright in September, Les Echos from 6% to 75%, and across the 294 publishers measured monthly since June those keeping any metadata rose from 60 to 67; France led October at 19.8 of 100, ahead of Germany at 19.2, with only countries of more than three scored publishers ranked (IPTC announcement).

Of 505 publishers whose policies were checked, 234 block at least one AI crawler in robots.txt, but 'robots.txt protects a website, not a photograph', and the PLUS Data Mining field appears on 0.6% of images (IPTC announcement); the archive's training-layer protocol holds that robots.txt and C2PA, which it does not call useless, operate 'primarily at the publication / legal / evidentiary layer rather than at the training-survival layer' (#127).

Leaving out the IPTC's own site, 27 of 6,580 images carried a C2PA manifest, all but one signed by an AI or design tool and none 'from a camera or a newsroom’s own signing', and seven carried a Digital Source Type disclosing generative-AI editing, so that, in the announcement's reading, provenance in news photography 'is arriving first through the tools that make synthetic images' (IPTC announcement); the per-field page finds DigitalSourceType on 0.2% of images and the AI prompt and AI system fields on none (Metawatch per-field breakdown), properties the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard added for AI-generated content on 27 November 2025 (Photo Metadata archive).

The archive's packet calls the adoption of artifact authenticity 'uneven' and C2PA's ingredient assertions 'optional, under-adopted' (#725), and its field manual holds that C2PA standards and watermarking have not 'achieved sufficient adoption to function as infrastructure' (#499).

The archive reads C2PA's trust as a device's: C2PA 'attests what a device reports having done' where a content-derived identifier 'computes what the bytes are', validation optional in the first, the two complementary (#1443), C2PA anchoring in device and issuer certificates and the AXN regime in content derivation and a public ledger (#1409), C2PA securing 'the camera's testimony, not the author's' (#1444).

It declares a nonsynthetic capture by the IPTC DigitalSourceType inside the file, 'in the same controlled vocabulary whose trainedAlgorithmicMedia value marks the synthetic class', and holds that 'C2PA, FADGI, and IPTC provenance vocabularies are the same insight arriving as standards' (#1409).

The monitor states its limits: the United States slipped from first to fourth in October because AP and USA Today 'began blocking automated access this month', 'a reminder that bot-blocking aimed at AI also shuts out research' (IPTC announcement; quoted in the census record's evidence, provenance census record), and publishers reached without a photograph are listed as no_images rather than scored zero, 'usually our blind spot rather than their practice' (Metawatch overview); the census record leaves unchecked 'the Metawatch site itself and its published run data' and IMATAG's 2018 study, and marks the monitor 'NOT a C2PA verifier' (provenance census record).

The archive holds the artifact dimension necessary and insufficient: C2PA 'prevents forgery; it does not constitute authorship' (#729), 'C2PA authenticates media' and does not cover text (#621), and 'When a 5,000-word article becomes a 200-word AI Overview, C2PA cannot tell you what was lost' (#615).

It finds that metadata standards, C2PA among them, do not address the measurable reception consequences of provenance and attribution (#833), that provenance and attribution studies, C2PA among them, 'have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs' (#1003), and that cross-format content provenance standards give 'starting points for the public and machine-readable layers' (#95).

On Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-29, the Capture Registry finds the method and scale right ('Every month', 'more than 500 news publishers in 122 countries' and the fields are the announcement's own) and 'Free and open' matched to the census record's licence quote, checked against that record and the pages it saved (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It finds the findings absent, 'The composition gives what the monitor checks and none of what it found', and the access limit not composed; it reads the Overview first as naming 'the maker, the method and the scale of a monitor three weeks old', then as composing 'A new provenance monitor' 'at the grain of its feature list', when what it measures is 'the erasure of credit in the publishing pipeline', carrying 'the instrument' and leaving out 'its reading', the IPTC photo metadata capture's pattern 'in small: the carrier composed, the loss omitted' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

At the capture the IPTC is named, Paul Melcher and Brendan Quinn appear only in cards, no identifier is given and the monitor's own pages are cited, and no card cites the census record, which landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The census record asks of each entity 'What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?', each quote verbatim from a saved source, and for Metawatch read one source, the announcement, on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record); Wikipedia has no article on IPTC Metawatch and no article text naming it beside the IPTC, and its article on the operator, which does not name Metawatch, describes the IPTC as 'a consortium of the world's major news agencies, other news providers and news industry vendors' acting as 'the global standards body of the news media', whose photo metadata, the IIM set that XMP has largely superseded, is 'by far IPTC's most widely used standard' (Wikipedia).

F31.quote: Even the best-populated field — Creator at 7.9% — appears on fewer than one in ten images we fetched. The fields most relevant to licensing ( WebStatement , LicensorURL ) are below 3%. The dataset as a whole tells a consistent story: publishers and CDNs are discarding metadata that the photographers and agencies almost certainly embedded upstream.

F11.quote: It isn’t the CDN’s fault. Images served through Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront and Fastly lost their metadata 87% to 95% of the time, but images served with no CDN at all also lost metadata 87% of the time. Stripping appears to happen in the publishing pipeline, which means that publishers can fix it.
F11.source_label: IPTC — Announcing Metawatch: a monthly check on which news publishers keep ... - IPTC

F18.quote: The fix is usually a setting, not a project. Most image pipelines strip metadata by default to save a few kilobytes; most can be told to keep it.

F15.quote: Of the 505 publishers whose policies we checked, 234 (46%) block at least one AI crawler in their robots.txt. … But robots.txt protects a website, not a photograph. … IPTC Photo Metadata has a field for exactly this: PLUS Data Mining . F16.quote: Leaving out IPTC’s own site, 27 of the 6,580 images we analysed carried a C2PA manifest, and all but one were signed by an AI or design tool: OpenAI, Adobe, Canva or Google (the last had a signer we couldn’t read). None came from a camera or a newsroom’s own signing.

O1443-01.quote: C2PA attests what a device reports having done. A content-derived identifier computes what the bytes are. The first requires trusting a chain of signers; the second requires trusting SHA-256. Validation is optional in the first and constitutive in the second.

O1443-02.quote: a trust model in which trust is extended to many entities by assumption and opt-in; **validation is not required by the specification** … These are **complementary rather than competing**

O1409-07.quote: C2PA anchors in device and issuer certificates, while the AXN regime anchors in content derivation plus an archive's public ledger, with the display-glyph checksum added so that integrity is legible to human readers as well as verifiers. The approaches are complementary

O1444-01.quote: **C2PA.** Capture-time provenance, camera-signed, platform-backed. It secures the camera's testimony, not the author's.
O1444-01.source_label: #1444 The Analog Advance: Operations Paper — Taking the Handwritten Niche (v1.0)

O729-02.quote: The Content Authenticity Initiative focuses on artifact provenance. A C2PA-signed text tells you what tool made it. It does not tell you whether the human is accountable for what was made. **C2PA prevents forgery; it does not constitute authorship.**
O729-02.source_label: #729 Provenance Is What Authorship Must Endure

O621-01.quote: **Against C2PA:** C2PA authenticates media. Doesn't cover text, doesn't handle multi-step AI generation, doesn't provide quality gradients, doesn't enforce governance.
O621-01.source_label: #621 Gravity Well Protocol Specification v1.0 — Governed Continuity for AI-Mediated Content (EA-GW-SPEC-01)

O615-01.quote: The Content Authenticity Initiative (C2PA) addresses media provenance — cryptographic manifests for images, video, and audio. This is valuable but narrowly scoped. It does not address what happens when textual meaning is compressed by a summarizer. When a 5,000-word article becomes a 200-word AI Overview, C2PA cannot tell you what was lost.
O615-01.source_label: #615 THE $650 BILLION GAP: Physical Infrastructure, Semantic Governance, and the Architecture of Compression-Survival

O833-01.quote: For *information science*, the dataset provides empirical evidence that provenance, attribution, and disambiguation have measurable reception consequences that existing metadata standards (Dublin Core, FAIR principles, C2PA) do not address.

O1003-01.quote: **Provenance and attribution studies** in digital environments — C2PA, the Data Provenance Initiative, W3C PROV — have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs.
O1003-01.source_label: #1003 AI-Native Intellectual Biography: Genre, Provenance, and the Archive That Outpaced Its Author Description (as recorded by DataCite)

O95-01.quote: Existing technical work on language-model watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al. 2023) and on cross-format content provenance standards (C2PA 2024) provides starting points for the public and machine-readable layers; the design space for the escrowed and internal-audit layers merits independent study.
